newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BellSouth, partners win big Brazil cellphone deal.
newsitem.headline: BellSouth, partners win big Brazil cellphone deal.

text.p: A group led by BellSouth Corp. and Brazilian bank Banco Safra won a lucrative cellular phone contract Wednesday covering the city of Sao Paulo with a $2.45 billion bid that staggered rivals and analysts by its size.

The BellSouth consortium, which also includes Brazilian media group O Estado de Sao Paulo and telecommunications equipment manufacturer Splice, left six other bidders in their tracks when it offered 2.647 billion reais for the 20-year concession.

The offer was more than four times the Communications Ministry's asking price of 600 million reais ($555 million) for the concession and 1.0 billion reais ($925 million) above the second highest bid. Analysts had expected the winning bid would be about 2.0 billion reais ($1.85 billion).
Some government officials said they believed the bid to the biggest ever made for a cellular phone concession. But members of the winning group played down suggestions they might have overpaid.

"The Sao Paulo market warrants this kind of investment," said Roberto Peon, BellSouth Latin America president. "It's one of the biggest investments in the world, but Sao Paulo is one of the most important cities in the world."

He said Sao Paulo, with its population of about 17 million, offered higher density of potential cellular phone users than Los Angeles and New York. The precarious state of conventional telephones would also add to the city's cellular potential.

"Paulistas are inseparable from cellphones, not like Americans who leave their phones in their cars," Peon said. "There are cultural reasons for the Latin American's love of cellphones. We prefer to be communicating all the time."
The group would invest up to $600 million over the next two years and planned to offer 400,000 lines within 12 months.

In the longer term, the consortium has its sights on a "good percentage" of the 800,000 to 1 million people believed to be waiting for a cellular telephone line in Sao Paulo, South America's largest city, Peon said.
Analysts noted that while the consortium's cash offer for the concession was much higher than those of rival bidders, its proposed tariffs were also far more expensive.

"We expected the winning bid to come in at about 2 billion reais ($1.85 billion)," said Alexandre Gartner, a telecommunications analyst with Rio investment bank Bozano, Simonsen. "But the group must have done its sums. Those tariffs are way higher than the rest."

The Sao Paulo city concession is the largest of 10 regional B Band frequency contracts being offered by the Brazilian government to attract much-needed capital to its ailing telecommunications sector.

Another, smaller B Band concession covering the northeastern states of Bahia and Sergipe was awarded Wednesday to a group led by Italy's state-owned telecommunications giant Stet and including Brazilian investors. It bid 250 million reais ($231 million) for the contract, 20 million reais ($18.5 million) above the government's asking price.
